summary:
Haggai is dated to the day: its four messages all fall in the second year of Darius king of Persia, 520 BC, within a span of four months (1:1; 2:1; 2:10; 2:20). Exiles back from Babylon had laid a foundation to replace the temple Nebuchadnezzar destroyed, but opposition stalled the work (Ezra 4:24), and people were saying, "The time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD" (1:2). The first message, to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, answers: "Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?" (1:4). "Consider carefully your ways," God says twice (1:5, 7): harvests fail and wages go into "a bag pierced through" (1:6) because the temple lies neglected (1:9–11). The people obey, God answers, "I am with you" (1:13), and work resumes twenty-three days later (1:15).

The second message is for those who remembered Solomon's temple, destroyed sixty-six years earlier: "Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How does it look to you now?" (2:3). God replies, "Work! For I am with you" (2:4), and promises, "Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth" (2:6, quoted in Hebrews 12:26) and "The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former" (2:9). The third message uses a priests' ruling on holiness and defilement to call the people's offerings defiled, then turns: "from this day on, I will bless you" (2:19). The fourth is for Zerubbabel alone: "I will make you like My signet ring" (2:23). A signet was a king's seal — the image God used when rejecting Zerubbabel's grandfather King Jehoiachin (Jeremiah 22:24).

The temple was finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15); Ezra 5:1 names the prophet Zechariah alongside Haggai in the work. This second temple, later enlarged by Herod the Great, is the temple of the Gospels.
